title: Tving CEO Says AI Likely Used in Data Breach, Admits She Didn't Verify Whether Security Spending Was Sufficient
source_used: Seoul Economic Daily (full text, AI-translated from Korean)
key_facts: Choi Joo-hee, chief executive of the South Korean streaming platform Tving, said at a National Assembly audit on 13 Oct 2026 that AI may have been used in a large-scale breach of customer personal data.
Asked by a People Power Party lawmaker whether the hack was AI-based, she said: "That is what we presume".
She said she did not make security enough of a priority to know whether Tving's investment was sufficient.
She said it has not been determined how the hacker first broke in; the National Police Agency is investigating the initial point of intrusion.
The Personal Information Protection Commission (PIPC) plans to complete its disciplinary action over the breach this year.
PIPC Chairperson Song Kyoung-hee said a fine is unlikely to be reduced simply because damages were paid if the compensation is not meaningful.
Gangnam Unni's operator, Healing Paper, also acknowledged security spending fell short of its growth, and Google Korea's head Yoon Gu said victim data was leaked by employee error.
quote_evidence: "That is what we presume," she said.
She added that "it has not yet been determined how the hacker first broke in," explaining that the National Police Agency is investigating the initial point of intrusion.
The Personal Information Protection Commission, the agency with jurisdiction over the case, plans to complete its disciplinary action over the Tving breach this year.
why_it_matters_hint: A company chief admits she did not check whether security spending was enough and presumes AI was used in a large customer-data theft.
notes: Article is AI-translated from Korean and warns quotes may not match the original wording. The AI claim is the CEO's presumption.
